lessonTitle: Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders: Hyponatraemia, Hyperkalaemia and Blood Gas Interpretation

blocks.text: A 68-year-old woman is brought to hospital by her daughter because she has become drowsy and confused over two days. She recently started a thiazide diuretic for blood pressure. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L. Nothing is wrong with her brain: the problem is in the water and salt balance of her blood, and the answer to how to treat her depends on whether she is dry, normal or waterlogged.

blocks.markdown: Sodium is the main extracellular cation, so **serum sodium concentration reflects water balance relative to sodium, not sodium content alone**. Hyponatraemia (serum sodium below about 135 mmol/L; ranges vary by laboratory) means too much water relative to sodium. Water moves into brain cells down the osmotic gradient, causing cerebral oedema, headache, confusion, seizures and coma, with symptoms worse if the fall is rapid.

blocks.caption: Calculated serum osmolality (mOsm/kg), with all concentrations in mmol/L. Doubling sodium accounts for its accompanying anions.

blocks.title: Is the low sodium hypotonic?
blocks.prompt: A patient has Na 124 mmol/L, glucose 6 mmol/L and urea 5 mmol/L. Calculate the osmolality and decide whether this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia.

steps.text: The normal range is about 275-295 mOsm/kg (laboratory dependent), so 259 is low.

A low serum osmolality confirms true hypotonic hyponatraemia, the group that needs a volume-status assessment. Hyponatraemia with normal osmolality suggests pseudohyponatraemia (for example severe hyperlipidaemia), and with high osmolality suggests water drawn out of cells by glucose or mannitol.

blocks.answer: Osmolality is about 259 mOsm/kg, so this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia.

blocks.markdown:
### Approach to hyponatraemia using volume status

Once hypotonic hyponatraemia is confirmed, assess **extracellular volume** clinically (skin turgor, mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure, oedema, orthostatic pressure) and use urine sodium and osmolality to refine the cause.

rows: Sodium loss exceeds water loss, with ADH stimulated by volume depletion
Renal loss (thiazides, Addison disease); extrarenal loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, burns)
Above about 30 mmol/L if renal loss; below about 20 mmol/L if extrarenal loss
Water retention with near-normal sodium; ADH inappropriately high or water excess
SIADH, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency, psychogenic polydipsia
Above about 30 mmol/L in SIADH; urine osmolality inappropriately high (above about 100)
Sodium and water retained, water more so; reduced effective arterial volume
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, advanced kidney disease
Below about 20 mmol/L (except advanced kidney disease)
blocks.caption: Hyponatraemia by volume status (cut-offs are guides)

blocks.title: Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly
blocks.text: In long-standing hyponatraemia brain cells have adapted by losing solutes. Rapid correction of sodium can cause osmotic demyelination, so correction rates are strictly limited. Treatment follows the cause and the severity of symptoms and is individualised.

blocks.markdown:
### Hyperkalaemia

Potassium is mostly intracellular, and the ratio of intracellular to extracellular potassium sets the resting membrane potential. A rise in serum potassium (above about 5.5 mmol/L; laboratory dependent) makes the resting potential less negative, which first excites then inactivates sodium channels and slows conduction, causing dangerous arrhythmias. Causes include reduced renal excretion (acute kidney injury, CKD), drugs (ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics), acidosis and tissue breakdown. **ECG changes progress with severity**: tall, tented (peaked) T waves, then flattened or absent P waves and a prolonged PR interval, then a widened QRS complex, and finally a sine-wave pattern leading to ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

rows: Antagonises the membrane effect and stabilises myocardium; does not lower potassium
Intravenous insulin with glucose; nebulised salbutamol
Stimulates Na-K ATPase and cellular uptake of potassium
blocks.caption: Emergency management of hyperkalaemia with ECG change (drugs are named as teaching examples, not advice)

blocks.markdown:
### Acid-base disorders and the arterial blood gas

The blood pH is held at about 7.35-7.45 (hydrogen ion concentration 35-45 nmol/L). The bicarbonate buffer system links pH to the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2, about 4.7-6.0 kPa or 35-45 mmHg) and bicarbonate (HCO3, about 22-26 mmol/L); reference values vary by laboratory. Interpret an arterial blood gas in steps: first the pH, to decide acidaemia or alkalaemia; second, which of PaCO2 or HCO3 moves in the direction explaining the pH change; third, whether the other value has moved in the compensating direction. Compensation never over-corrects the pH.

rows: Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea
blocks.caption: Four primary acid-base disorders
Anion gap (mmol/L). A typical reference range is about 8-12 mmol/L without potassium, varying by laboratory.

blocks.title: Interpreting a blood gas
blocks.prompt: A patient has pH 7.28, PaCO2 8.9 kPa and HCO3 31 mmol/L. Interpret.

steps.text: pH 7.28 is below 7.35, so there is acidaemia.
PaCO2 of 8.9 kPa is high, and carbon dioxide retention is acidifying, so the primary disorder is respiratory acidosis.
HCO3 is raised at 31, which is the renal compensation, and since the pH is still below normal the compensation is incomplete.

blocks.answer: Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic (renal) compensation, as seen in chronic ventilatory failure.

blocks.title: A raised anion gap points to added acid
blocks.text: In metabolic acidosis, a high anion gap indicates accumulation of an unmeasured acid such as lactate, ketones, uraemic acids or toxins. A normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic acidosis) suggests bicarbonate loss, for example from diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis.

points: Hyponatraemia is a water excess relative to sodium; confirm it is hypotonic, then use volume status and urine sodium to find the cause (hypovolaemic, euvolaemic such as SIADH, or hypervolaemic).

Hyperkalaemia produces peaked T waves, flat P waves, widened QRS and sine-wave rhythms, and the emergency response is calcium to protect the heart, insulin with glucose and salbutamol to shift potassium, and removal from the body.
An ABG is read stepwise by pH, then the primary respiratory or metabolic change, then compensation, with the anion gap characterising metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer has serum sodium 121 mmol/L. He appears euvolaemic with no oedema. Urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 62 mmol/L. Serum osmolality is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

questions.correctOptionText: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium is SIADH.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: polydipsia gives dilute urine (low osmolality).
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: he is euvolaemic and vomiting would give low urine sodium.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: serum osmolality is low, so this is true hyponatraemia.

questions.explanation: In SIADH ADH acts inappropriately, so water is retained and urine remains concentrated despite low plasma osmolality. Small-cell lung cancer is a classic ectopic source of ADH.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has leg oedema and serum sodium 126 mmol/L. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L. Which classification and mechanism fit best?

options.text: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia with reduced effective arterial volume driving sodium and water retention
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from renal sodium loss
Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia from advanced kidney disease

questions.correctOptionText: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia with reduced effective arterial volume driving sodium and water retention

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ascites and oedema show total body overload, while low effective arterial volume activates RAAS and ADH, so urine sodium is low.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: he has oedema and ascites, not volume depletion, and urine sodium is low rather than high.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: oedema indicates hypervolaemia, not euvolaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: advanced kidney disease would usually give a high urine sodium.

questions.explanation: In cirrhosis, splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume. The kidney responds by retaining sodium and water, with water retention proportionately greater, causing dilutional hyponatraemia with a low urine sodium.

questions.stem: Which is generally the earliest ECG change seen as serum potassium rises?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: peaked T waves are the earliest sign of hyperkalaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: U waves are a feature of hypokalaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: diffuse ST elevation suggests pericarditis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: hyperkalaemia prolongs, not shortens, the PR interval as it progresses.

questions.explanation: Rising extracellular potassium accelerates repolarisation, producing tall, narrow, tented T waves. With further rise, P waves flatten, the PR interval lengthens and the QRS widens.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a serum potassium of 7.4 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which treatment should be given first to reduce the immediate risk of arrhythmia?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes, although it does not lower potassium.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: resins act slowly and do not protect the heart acutely.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: saline alone does not rapidly protect the myocardium.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid and is not an emergency treatment.

questions.explanation: ECG changes mean the myocardium is at risk of life-threatening arrhythmia, so membrane stabilisation with calcium comes first. Insulin with glucose and salbutamol then shift potassium into cells, and definitive removal follows.

questions.stem: A patient has pH 7.31, PaCO2 3.2 kPa and HCO3 12 mmol/L. Which interpretation is correct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low pH and low bicarbonate indicate metabolic acidosis, and the low PaCO2 reflects compensatory hyperventilation.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: respiratory acidosis would have a high PaCO2.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the pH is acidic, not alkaline.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a low PaCO2 here is the compensation, not the primary process, since the pH is low.

questions.explanation: The pH is low, so the primary problem is an acidosis, and the bicarbonate is low, which identifies it as metabolic. The respiratory system has lowered PaCO2 to partly restore pH.

questions.stem: A patient has serum sodium 138 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L and bicarbonate 12 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap in mmol/L, without including potassium.
questions.explanation: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 138 - (98 + 12) = 28 mmol/L. This is well above the typical range of about 8-12, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from an unmeasured acid.

questions.stem: A patient has serum sodium 128 mmol/L, glucose 5 mmol/L and urea 7 mmol/L. Using osmolality = 2[Na] + [glucose] + [urea], calculate the serum osmolality in mOsm/kg.
questions.explanation: Osmolality = 2 x 128 + 5 + 7 = 256 + 12 = 268 mOsm/kg. This is below the normal range of about 275-295, confirming hypotonic hyponatraemia, so the next step is to assess volume status.

questions.stem: Outline a diagnostic approach to a patient found to have a serum sodium of 120 mmol/L.
markingGuide: Confirm true hypotonic hyponatraemia by measuring or calculating serum osmolality, excluding pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia
Assess extracellular volume clinically: hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or hypervolaemic
Hypovolaemic: renal loss (thiazides, Addison disease) versus extrarenal loss (vomiting, diarrhoea) separated by urine sodium
Euvolaemic: SIADH, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency, polydipsia; urine osmolality and sodium
Hypervolaemic: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome with low urine sodium
Mention of slow correction to avoid osmotic demyelination
questions.explanation: The sodium concentration says nothing about volume, so the systematic approach separates dilution from depletion before treatment. Treatment follows the cause and must avoid over-rapid correction.

questions.stem: Describe the ECG changes of hyperkalaemia in order of increasing severity, and explain the rationale for each step of the emergency treatment.
markingGuide: Flattened or absent P waves and prolonged PR interval
Widened QRS complex then sine-wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation or asystole
Calcium: stabilises myocardial membrane, does not lower potassium
Insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol: shift potassium into cells
Removal: loop diuretics, potassium binders or dialysis, treating the cause
questions.explanation: Rising extracellular potassium depolarises the resting membrane and slows conduction, so ECG changes mark the danger of arrhythmia. Treatment is staged: protect the heart, shift potassium temporarily, then remove it from the body.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman during a panic attack has pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.0 kPa and HCO3 22 mmol/L. Interpret the blood gas step by step, name two other causes of this disorder, and explain why the bicarbonate is only slightly altered.
markingGuide: Low PaCO2 explains the alkalosis, so primary respiratory alkalosis; bicarbonate near normal
Other causes: pain, pulmonary embolism, high altitude, early salicylate poisoning, anxiety
Renal compensation takes days to develop, so in acute respiratory alkalosis bicarbonate has barely changed
questions.explanation: The pH is alkaline and the low carbon dioxide accounts for it, so the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Renal compensation by bicarbonate excretion is slow, so an acute disturbance shows little change in bicarbonate.
